description: Student developer team building interactive web experiences. We’re interested in space, games, and technology. For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, we want to create a fun lunar/Mars outpost simulation. Looking for teammates skilled in game development, UI/UX, design, animation, space science, or education.
summary:
Our project is an interactive Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer that turns the challenges of lunar and Martian exploration into an engaging learning experience. We developed a browser-based simulation where students take the role of mission commanders, managing an outpost while balancing essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, power, and radiation protection.

Every decision has consequences. Players must make strategic choices, respond to unexpected mission events, and understand how using one resource can affect another. Through interactive gameplay, students experience the real engineering trade-offs involved in keeping astronauts safe and sustaining a space mission.

Our project addresses NASA's challenge by transforming complex space exploration concepts into an accessible, hands-on experience for children aged 7–12. It is important because it makes STEM education more engaging, encourages critical thinking and problem-solving, and helps the next generation understand the science and decisions behind humanity's future beyond Earth.
details:
Our project is an interactive space mission simulation designed to help students understand the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players take the role of mission commanders and make decisions about essential resources such as oxygen, power, food, water, and radiation protection. Every decision has consequences: allocating more power to life support may leave less available for scientific experiments, while improving radiation shielding may require sacrificing other resources.

The project turns complex space engineering concepts into an accessible and engaging learning experience for students aged 7–12. Through interactive scenarios, resource management, and mission events, players learn why astronauts and mission planners must carefully balance limited resources to keep a crew alive and a mission successful. Players can experiment with different strategies, experience the consequences of poor decisions, and try again with a better understanding of the challenges.

The intended impact is to make space science and engineering more understandable and exciting for younger students. Rather than simply reading about lunar and Martian exploration, students actively experience the decisions involved in surviving beyond Earth. The project aims to encourage scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, resource awareness, and an interest in STEM careers.

The project was developed using modern web technologies, including React, TypeScript, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Python and FastAPI for backend functionality where applicable. We also explored NASA's publicly available scientific resources and datasets as a foundation for making the simulation more realistic. The application is designed as a browser-based experience to make it accessible without requiring specialized hardware or software installations.

What makes our approach creative is the combination of game mechanics and real-world space exploration challenges. Instead of presenting space science as a collection of facts, we turn it into a series of decisions where resources are interconnected and every choice involves a trade-off. We considered the target audience's age, accessibility, educational value, scientific accuracy, gameplay balance, and the importance of making complex concepts understandable without oversimplifying the real challenges of space exploration.
